questions.q: What is the programme mainly about?
options: Healthy food to eat with the family
How to set a dinner table quickly
How people talk and behave around the dinner table
Why families no longer eat their meals together at home
questions.why: Neil says they're not interested in food but in talking at the dinner table.

questions.q: What does Neil say about eating at the table as a child?
options: His family rarely ate together
He had to eat in silence
He always had to eat at a separate children's table in the kitchen
It was often the only time the family could chat together
questions.why: He says it was an important daily ritual and often the only time they could get together and chat.

questions.q: Why does Neil value family meals with his own children?
options: The children eat more vegetables
The children open up more about their day
It is the only time he cooks
The children learn good table manners from him
questions.why: He says the kids are more likely to open up about their day or something troubling them.

questions.q: What does Philippa Perry say happens in any group?
options: We take on a role, like “the funny one”
We always become the leader
We stop being ourselves completely in every group
We start arguing with each other
questions.why: She says in any group we find a role, such as the funny one or the wise one.

questions.q: What is Philippa Perry's advice about the role you have in your family?
options: Accept it, because your family members always know you best
Try to change it by arguing
Don't believe it too much, as it may not be who you are
Only show that side of yourself at home
questions.why: She says take an assigned family role “with a little bit of a pinch of salt”.

questions.q: How were children sometimes treated at the table in the past?
options: They sat apart from adults or were expected to stay quiet
They were usually allowed to lead the conversation at meals
They served food to the adults
They ate before everyone else
questions.why: Beth says children sometimes sat at a different table or were told to be seen and not heard.

questions.q: How do older relatives react to Ambreia Meadows-Fernandez's children's questions?
options: They get angry with the children and leave the table
They refuse to answer
They find them boring
Mostly positively, though it can be a bit of a shock
questions.why: She says it's a mixed bag – overwhelmingly positive, but a bit of a culture shock.

questions.q: According to Ambreia, why are her children's questions a surprise to older people?
options: Her children are much older than they look and act like adults
They weren't raised with separate adult and kid tables
Her children speak a different language
Her children only ask about food
questions.why: She says her kids weren't raised with that line between the adult table and the kid table.
